*Tattvasaṃgrahaḥ*, composed by Sadyojyotiḥ Śivācārya.

I bow to the illustrious Abhra Sabhāpati, the bestower of all things, whose stainless state of Śiva-hood is eternal and distinct from the entire universe, and who is accompanied by the commentary composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
The supreme teacher Sadyojyotis, who was an expert in grammar, logic, and epistemology,
possessed such vast power of intellect that we perceived him as if he were Śiva himself.
The Bṛhaṭṭīkā, an autumnal night, has been spread forth by the illustrious Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha for the illumination of the moon that is the Tattvasaṃgraha.
Nevertheless, for the benefit of those whose intellects are weary by the extensive Great Commentary, this concise commentary is here composed by me.
In this regard, first of all, our venerable teacher, preceded by a prostration to Paramaśiva, declares his intention to compose this treatise:
"Having prostrated before Śaṅkara— the unborn, omniscient leader of the conscious and the unconscious— I [shall compose this work]."
For the sake of awakening those of dull intellect, I shall speak of the principles in brief. || 1 ||

The meaning is that He is the leader and presiding controller of both the conscious (cit), which consists of bound souls, and the unconscious (acit), which consists of the *bindu*, *māyā*, and their effects;

and by being the material cause of the pure and impure worlds, both directly and through a lineage, He bestows pure and impure enjoyments upon souls as is appropriate for each. And therefore, because the world possesses a specific arrangement and so forth, it is an effect.

The intended meaning is that the existence of God is established by His being the agent of that [creation]. By this, those who maintain the doctrine of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), karma, and God are also refuted;
for primordial matter and karma are insentient, and the individual soul, being possessed of impurity, is not independent. It is "unborn" (*aja*) because it is eternally pure.
It is devoid of birth even in the form of association with a body and so forth. By this, its eternity is established. For of this—

If the creator of the world were non-eternal or subject to birth and so forth, he would necessarily be insentient and there would be an infinite regress. Furthermore, he is omniscient because he is free from impurity and is the creator of all things. The underlying intention here is this: his knowledge does not depend on the conjunction of the mind and other factors as it does for the Naiyāyikas and others; rather, knowledge is his very nature. And of that [knowledge]...
The infinity [of consciousness] is merely figurative, arising from the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the objects of knowledge and their effects. As it is heard in scripture:
"That [consciousness], though one, attains an infinity of divisions due to the infinity of its objects;
and because it is non-different from them, its agency likewise follows figuratively, just like that [infinity]."

(Mṛgendravṛtti 5.17) He is Śaṅkara because he bestows upon the selves a state of equality with himself—consisting of bliss (*śam*), which is of the nature of being unimpelled, and comprising omniscience and omnipotence. By this, he declares his status as the bestower of liberation; furthermore, this is the term that designates the goal. To him who is thus constituted...

Having bowed to the Blessed One and being humble in body, speech, and mind, I shall speak briefly of the principles (tattvas), such as earth and the rest. The meaning is that the definition of these principles is the subject matter (abhidheya) of this work. To the question "For what purpose is this begun?", he says: "for those of dull intellect. The intention is as follows: [this is for the sake of those] who have been taught by Mataṅga and others...

Because the definition of reality (*tattva*) is extremely extensive, it is impossible for those of dull intellect to comprehend it; therefore, this [work] is commenced for the sake of providing them with a concise understanding of reality. Furthermore, since the knowledge of reality is the means—through a traditional succession—to both the higher and lower liberation, the purpose consisting of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) is also indicated herein. And thus:

The relationship between the *Tattvajñāna-prakaraṇa* (the section on the knowledge of reality) and [the other sections] is established as that of the signified and the signifier; furthermore, the relationship between the knowledge of reality and liberation is established as that of the means and the end. He will also describe the relationship consisting of the lineage of teachers (*gurusaṃpradāya*), stating: "The Blessed One, the supreme light, the omniscient one, has shown favor. Since "favor" (*anugraha*) is illustrative, [this applies] from Paramaśiva onwards.
The meaning is that the established doctrine (siddhāntārtha) is firmly grounded through an unbroken lineage of scriptural tradition reaching back to the Self. || 1 ||

Having thus promised an exposition of the principles (*tattva*), [the author] now proceeds to present them in reverse order for the sake of attaining Śiva, according to the venerable *Svāyambhuva-śruti*, which indicates that purification occurs through initiation (*dīkṣā*) precisely by way of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Thus, he first describes the five elements in the order of withdrawal: 1. Earth (*pṛthivī*) 2. Water (*ap*) 3. Fire (*tejas*) 4. Wind (*vāyu*) 5. Ether (*ākāśa*) [The text continues with the definitions of these elements.]
The functions of these elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—are, respectively:
supporting, cohesion, ripening, expansion, and providing room. (2)

The meaning is that the elements (*bhūta*) are indeed earth, water, fire, air, and ether. He states that the perfection [of these] comes from their respective functions, such as supporting, and so forth, by saying "of these, in order. Among those, *saṃgraha* (cohesion) is support;
*vyūha* (arrangement) is the joining together of parts; and the function of space (*ākāśa*) is the granting of room, which is its locus. From that...

Since space is established through its functional effect consisting in the granting of room (*avakāśa*), the Cārvākas—who deny its existence—and the Mīmāṃsakas—who claim it is perceptible—are refuted. Furthermore, its eternity is not asserted as it is by the Naiyāyikas and others, because, as will be explained later, it is an effect of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and because of the scriptural statement regarding its being the support of the world; moreover, the term "manifestation" (*vyūha*) is also an indication for the effects of air.

As they say: "Wind is characterized by touch, sound, support, and motion. Furthermore: "Smell, taste, form, touch, and sound are the five qualities of earth; among those of water and the others, each preceding one is omitted in succession. As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "Thus, this sound exists in the five [elements], and touch in the four elements; in earth and wind, [touch] is neither cold nor hot, while in [water and fire] it is cold and hot [respectively]."

"In water and fire; in the sun and fire it is bright; in water it is white; on earth it is manifold, such as white and so forth. Color exists in these three [elements]. Taste is in water; in earth it is sixfold. Smell is on earth; it is considered by the wise to be both non-fragrant and fragrant. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.27–29).
For this very reason, that which was stated by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—that sound is a unique quality of space because it is perceived elsewhere than its substrate—is [refuted].
That which is illogical is so because its reason (*hetu*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), being sublated by perception and scripture.

For instance, by perception, an echo is heard in space; the rustling sound in the wind; the crackling sound in fire; the splashing sound in water; and the clattering sound in earth. Furthermore, sounds are also perceived in their substrates, such as drums and the like.
This and more has been explained by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. || 2 ||

And since those elements possess qualities that can be discerned by the external sense organs of beings such as ourselves—just like a jar or other objects—it is established that they must have a cause; thus, their cause, the five *tanmātras*, is established. He says:
"The cause possesses qualities identical to those elements, and it is the filler of that very [element]."
For this is the distinction of the primary element (bhūta): it consists of that alone, yet it is devoid of specific qualities (viśeṣa).

The *tanmātra*, possessing qualities identical to those of its corresponding element (*bhūta*), serves as that element’s cause, its material source (*upādāna*), its filler, and its nourisher—this is the remainder [of the statement]. As they say: "The function of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the production of what has not yet been produced and the augmentation of what has already been produced. And therefore:

The subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), which consists of the five qualities beginning with smell, is the cause of earth; the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), consisting of the four qualities beginning with taste, is the cause of water, and so on for the others clearly. By this, the Naiyāyikas and others who assert that these [subtle elements] exist in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*) are refuted; for, being insentient, multiple, and corporeal, they would be like jars and other such objects.

Or rather, because it is an effect, like dust and so forth, it does not deviate from that nature. Therefore, we shall explain that through the medium of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the rest, Māyā alone is the supreme cause. If this is so, since the gross elements and the subtle elements possess identical qualities, what is the distinction between them? To this he says: "The subtle element [is the cause] of the gross element. For just as the qualities such as odor and the rest reside in the gross elements like earth and so forth, [so too do they reside in their respective subtle elements].

They are perceived as possessing specific qualities (*viśiṣṭa*) as previously described, but this is not the case with their causes, the *tanmātras*. Therefore, because they consist of mere unqualified qualities due to their subtlety, the class of gross elements (*bhūtavarga*) possesses a distinction consisting in its connection with specific qualities due to its grossness. For this very reason, these are designated by the name *tanmātra*. Thus it is heard:
"The tanmātras, distinguished by their qualities, are joined with the term 'tanmātra'. (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 12.5). || 3 ||
Now, he states that these elements (bhūtas) and subtle elements (tanmātras) are denoted by the term "effect" (kārya) and serve as the substrata for the sense organs:
"This effect is tenfold; having entered [the body] through the instruments (karaṇas), it is made to perform activity.
But because they are not all-pervading (avibhutva), the instruments, having taken hold of the effect, perform their activity. (Verse 4)

And it is stated in the Mataṅga that these exist as the supports of the senses in both gross and subtle forms: "In this world, the subtle elements (tanmātras) are like a jar, and the great elements (mahābhūtas) are like a coating" (Viśeṣa-pāda 19.21). || 4 ||
Now he states the accomplishment of the organs of action: the organs of action are speech, grasping, excretion, pleasure, and locomotion;
the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the organs of cognition. (5)

The instruments (karaṇa) are designated as speech, hands, feet, the organ of generation, and the anus. "Excretion" refers to the elimination of waste. The meaning is that speech and the other organs are established as instruments for the actions of speaking and so forth. Consequently, the Naiyāyikas and others who deny the existence of the organs of action are refuted, because no action is possible without an instrument.

If it is objected that since the raising of the eyebrow-creeper and so forth are also actions, there would follow the consequence of an infinite number of organs of action (*karmendriya*), we say: no. This is because those [faculties] are not admitted to pervade the entire body like the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*); rather, the activities such as the raising of the eyebrows are attributed to specific names based on the respective powers of the various senses located in those particular places, such as the hands.

There is no contradiction because of the specific basis [of the term]. The sense organs are stated as "the ear, the sense of touch," and so forth. That by which one touches is the *sparśana*, namely the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*). Vision (*darśana*) is also simply the eye (*cakṣus*). || 5 ||
Now, he explains by what operations their accomplishment occurs:
"The function (*vṛtti*) of these [organs] with respect to each of the objects, beginning with sound, is mere observation (*ālocana*).
Thus, the external instrument is tenfold, being distinct from the functions of desire, exertion, and cognition. (6)
The internal organ is threefold, to be designated as mind (citta), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi).
From the ego arise the mind, the external organs, and the elemental sources. (7)

The function (*vṛtti*) of these [senses], the ear and so forth, is respectively the observation (*ālocana*), that is, the grasping, of their objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. This is the specific, non-common function of each. The point is that their existence is established by the fact that the apprehension of sound and the other objects would otherwise be impossible.
Thus...
The remainder [of the verse] indicates that the external sense organ is to be known as being of ten kinds. He states the establishment of the internal organ with the words "the internal organ.

The internal organ is threefold, distinct from the external organs, and is designated as mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). He states that their functions are, respectively, desire and so forth, with the words "having the functions of desire, exertion, and cognition. Among these, by the word "desire" (*icchā*)—

Attention, termed *saṃkalpa* and synonymous with one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), is said to exist. And because it consists of vision and action, it is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which are their effects and consist of the reflective awareness of external subjects; for those two are of the nature of cognitions.
Therefore, that of which this is the effect is the mind (*manas*); thus is the proof of the mind. And that mind [is characterized] by internal volition (*saṃkalpa*).

And it is stated in the *Mataṅga* that the mind has a twofold function by means of presiding over the external senses: "That mind, which effects the experience for the enjoyer, possesses a twofold function because it always acts through the state of being external organs in a manner appropriate to itself. Furthermore, the capacity of the senses is produced by the volition residing within [the self]; therefore, the mind is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). (Viṣṇu Purāṇa)

Thus [it is said] in the *Mṛgendra*: "The initiator of the gods, moving swiftly, and having the nature of volition" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 12.7). And there, by the word "gods" (*deva*), the sense organs (*indriya*) are meant. Furthermore, the fact that [the Self] presides over the sense organs is established in that very same work:
"Since there is never any activity when the Self, the sense organs, and the objects are not in proximity, the existence of an agent of activity is determined even through reasoning. (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā*)

(12.9). Thus, because it is non-omnipresent, restricted to each individual self, and manifold, the mind is an effect. Likewise, *saṃrambha* (impulse), which consists of effort (*prayatna*), is indeed an effect of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). As it has been said: "Impulse is a function of the ego-sense" (Bhoga-kārikā 33).
And that [impulse] is [produced] by that which serves as the substratum for the power of cognition...

It exists as the substratum for the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) which possesses the determination toward awakening (*bodha*). This very [power] is the cause for the activity of the internal wind (*vāyu*) in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. As they say: "How could there be the impelling and drawing of the wind without effort? (*Pratyakṣapariccheda* 1.54). Furthermore, because it is the effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature consists in the reflective awareness of the object of perception (*grāhyaparāmarśa*).

The proof of *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-principle) is as follows: that which is the instrument for the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I," which is unitary in form yet extremely distinct from the manifold forms [of objects] that arise at every moment, is *ahaṅkāra*. Furthermore, this is not the effect of the other *tattvas* (principles), because those are established by their own respective effects, and because there is no evidence for its being the cause of any other effect; moreover, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to postulate an infinite number of *tattvas*. Thus...

Cognition (*bodha*) is the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) consisting of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object of apprehension. For it is thus: here, cognition is of two kinds—of the nature of determination and of the nature of non-determination. Among these, that which is of the nature of non-determination always appears solely in the form of the subject (*grāhaka*) and is the very essence of the Self (*ātman*). However, that which is of the nature of determination...

That which appears as impermanent due to its arising and occurrence does not have the nature of a person (*pums*), because it is impossible for that which is eternal to possess the nature of the impermanent.

Nor is this [person] experienced as eternal; therefore, that whose nature this [cognition] is, is the intellect (*buddhi*). As they say: "There is indeed an initial non-conceptualizing awareness of mere observation, similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth, which arises from the pure object."

"Furthermore, that cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth is also accepted as perception" (*Ślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣa 112, 120). Moreover, the establishment of the intellect (*buddhi*) is heard [in scripture] as being the substratum of *dharma* and other qualities: "The states (*bhāva*)—virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and power (*aiśvarya*)—are the qualities of the intellect; they are *sāttvika*, or these [same qualities] are the opposite [when *tāmasa*]."

"Having abandoned passion, [the Tamasic ones remain]. (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 10.24). This is the intended meaning: since action, consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), perishes at the very moment of its performance, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called *apūrva* (the unprecedented) must be postulated as its product, because otherwise the scriptural teaching of results occurring at a later time would be inexplicable. Furthermore, that [impression] cannot reside in the Self (*ātman*).

Because [the self] is unchanging, and because actions such as agriculture are seen to effect a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the self, [the self] is indeed merely insentient (*jaḍa*). That in which those [actions] produce a refinement is the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses the eight qualities beginning with *dharma*. The same should be said regarding the refinements of knowledge and so forth.
And it has been stated elsewhere that these dispositions (*bhāva*) number three hundred, according to the distinctions among the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) such as *siddhi* and the rest.

Having thus established the group of instruments (the organs), he explains from what their origin arises: "Their origin is from the *ahaṅkāra*. Therein, the origin of the mind and the sense-organs (*buddhīndriyas*) is from the *ahaṅkāra*-aggregate known as *taijasa*, which is characterized by *sattva*;

that of the organs of action (*karmendriyas*) is from the one known as *vaikārika*, which is characterized by *rajas*; and that of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the source of the gross elements, is from the one characterized by *tamas*.
The origin of these [organs] is from the threefold *ahaṅkāra*, beginning with the *bhūtādi* (the elemental).
As it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose, together with the mind—these are *sāttvika* due to their connection with illumination (*prakāśa*);
that [type of *ahaṅkāra*] is the *taijasa* (luminous) and *sāttvika*. Speech, hands, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet—these arise from *rajas*."

Due to the continuity of karma, that group here which is predominantly *rajas* is the *vaikārika*. Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these subtle elements (*tanmātras*), distinguished by their qualities and designated by the term "subtle element," arise from *tamas*. This is because they differ from the groups that perform illumination and action, and because they are themselves objects of illumination among the [products of] the *ahaṃkāra* known as *bhūtādi*.

"...is tāmasa" (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.3–6). Therefore, through the door of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*), the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of the Self is manifested by the *taijasa* ego; likewise, through the door of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is manifested by the *vaikārika* ego. Because of its impurity, [the latter] is considered inferior to the former. Furthermore, the designation of these as *sāttvika* and so forth is due to the predominance of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva*.
According to the principle that "that which transforms does not transform unmixed," it is not, however, the producer of a single [effect]. || 6-7 ||
The birth of the Great Principle (mahat) and of the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises from the three qualities (guṇas);
these are sattva, rajas, and tamas, which take the forms of illumination, activity, and restraint.

The birth of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is from the intellect (*buddhi*), and the birth of the intellect is from the principle of the *guṇas*. This has also been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "From primordial nature (*prakṛti*) comes the Great One (*mahat*); from that, the ego; from that, the group of sixteen" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 22). Now, it may be argued that the Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that the sense organs are material (*bhautika*) because they have restricted objects. That is incorrect, because [the senses] such as the eye...
This is because a quality residing in one element is perceived by other elements, as well as through the commonality of action; as it has been stated in the *Bhogakārikās*:

"And because they are composed of the elements, if there were a restriction regarding action and commonality, then cognitions would clearly not arise from the gods for embodied beings, even in the case of their inherent connection" (verse 40). As for what was said—that despite the lack of distinction in their status as causal factors (*kāraka*), these [cognitions] do not [arise]— [The text continues: ...because of the non-distinction in their being causal factors, yet this is not so for them... [the rest of the passage is omitted in the source].

As for the claim that there is a distinction in their inherent natures determined by their respective objects, that too will be like the distinction between the products of sugarcane—such as molasses, candied sugar, and granulated sugar—which arises from differences in their production; therefore, this argument amounts to nothing. Now he states the principle of the *guṇas*: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas. This means that illumination, activity, and restraint are, respectively, the functions of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*. And through these [functions], by means of the subtle body...

Pervasiveness exists in all the effects of *māyā*. Furthermore, "illumination" (*prakāśa*) and the others are indicative of the other subordinate functions of the *guṇas*. For instance, it is stated in the *Mataṅga* and other texts that stability, fortitude, and so forth are functions of *sattva*;
cruelty, heroism, and so forth are functions of *rajas*; and lack of interest, dullness, and so forth are functions of *tamas*.
Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the *guṇas* themselves are *prakṛti*; [the author] says this is incorrect:
"Those three *guṇas* here are indeed those whose origination is from the Unmanifest;
for the non-differentiation of the *guṇas* must necessarily exist in their substrate, just like the portions of earth and so forth. (9)

The intended meaning is as follows: since the *guṇas* are insentient and manifold, they must be preceded by a cause—just like jars and other such objects—and therefore their origin is from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) alone; thus, the word "eva" (alone) is placed out of its logical order [to emphasize this]. He elaborates on the fact that they are effects of *prakṛti* with the words "the support" (*ādhāra*). Just as the portions of earth and so forth, which take the form of jars and the like, have the earth as their essence...

In a substratum, non-distinction necessarily exists; likewise, it must be understood that there is necessarily non-distinction among the constituent parts of the qualities (guṇas), such as *sattva* and the others, within some substratum. Therefore, that which is the substratum of this non-distinction is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); thus is the proof of the Unmanifest established. This has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*: "Therefore, the principle of Pradhāna..."
"From the *kalātattva* it produced that which is the secondary cause (*gauṇakāraṇa*) for the one who possesses the seven knots. (Vijñānabhairava 10.19). Thus [ends the section]. 9.

Immediately thereafter, he states the establishment of the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*): "In this system, that activity directed toward a man as an object of enjoyment, which arises from attachment, is passion.
For if passion were merely [attachment] toward a specific object of enjoyment, no one would ever be free from passion. (10)
But is it not the case that in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, the *puruṣatattva* is heard of as being situated between *prakṛti* and *rāga*? That is true;
however, because it is sentient and eternal, it cannot constitute a *adhvan* (path) by virtue of being the substratum for worlds and so forth.

For instance, there is a connection with the five principles beginning with *kalā* through the impurity of *puṃstva* (the state of being a subject), which consists of the ego-inflation (*abhimāna*) regarding the non-self and so forth as being the self.

Since it is introduced in the Āgamas for the purpose of its purification at that very place during initiation (*dīkṣā*), its recitation is heard [in the scriptures] subsequently as the *puruṣatattva*. For this reason, the Teacher has omitted its description here. However, immediately after the *māyātattva*, he will describe the nature of the bound soul (*paśu*). In this person (*puruṣa*), by which [agency] desire is produced for the sake of seizing objects of enjoyment...

Activity occurs; this is to be understood here in the Śaiva scripture as *rāga* (attachment). The meaning is that the reality-principle (*tattva*) of *rāga* is established through its effect, which is the nature of longing (*abhilāṣa*). Now, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that longing, characterized by the absence of dispassion (*avairāgya*), is merely a quality of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) and thus the cause [of activity]; however, that is incorrect, because a latent impression (*vāsanā*) in its form as a mere potentiality does not produce an effect, and if it were to produce an effect, it would belong to the intellect.

Furthermore, because of the constant association with infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of a person simultaneously experiencing an infinite number of contradictory cognitions.

Even that which has the form of direct perception cannot be the cause of desire, as it is itself an object of enjoyment. Now, one might argue that the excellence of the object itself must be the cause of desire; but that is not so, for if desire were to arise from the mere proximity of the object, everyone would become passionate, leading to the absurd conclusion that no one could ever be free from passion. Therefore:

Since the vision of one free from passion would otherwise be impossible, it must be admitted that there exists a passion residing in the subject (*grāhaka*) which serves as the cause of desire. This very point is stated [in the verse]:

"the specific object of enjoyment" (*bhogyaviśeṣa*). Nor should it be argued that karma alone will be the coloring agent (*rañjaka*), because its purpose is fulfilled solely in the production of results, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of postulating many distinct principles (*tattva*). [Objection: But surely the nature of Māyā is to delude?
Let there be passion; that is not so, because illusion does not cause delusion directly, but rather only through its effects—thus there is no fault.

And that one who is free from passion (vītarāga) is indeed established by direct perception; thus he says: "When there is attachment toward a limited object, that [attachment] is not seen when the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is vast.
Therefore, it should not be said of us that 'there is no one free from passion who possesses distinctions'. (11)

Since that desire is not observed with respect to a particular object such as a woman even when the latent impression (*upadhāna*) exists, one must not say—on the grounds of its being perceived through direct perception—that there is no distinct state of freedom from passion characterized by the absence of desire. || 11 ||

He states the attainment of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva): "That by which the person, having impelled the Great One (mahat) and the other [evolutes], makes the object of experience an experience, and which [further] effects the experience within that object of experience—that is Knowledge; it is the supreme instrument. (12)

By means of which instrument the Puruṣa, having impelled the entire collection of instruments such as the intellect (buddhi) and the ego (ahaṅkāra), brings about the object of experience (bhogya), and within that object of experience effects the actual experience—that instrument called "knowledge" (vidyā) is said to be "supreme" (para) because of its proximity to the Self. This is what is meant: [it is like] by means of a horse, a road, and a lamp...

Just as in the case of [the verb] "he goes" (*yāti*) and so forth, even though the fruit here is accomplished by many instruments, knowledge alone is the supreme instrument, because by that alone one knows the object of experience. || 12 ||
What, then, is the object of enjoyment here, and what is enjoyment? To this he says:
In brief, the intellect (*buddhi*), taking the form of objects and consisting of pleasure and so forth, is the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*).
Enjoyment (*bhoga*) is the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-vyakti*) of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) when it is reflected in the object of enjoyment. (13)

The intellect (*buddhi*) itself—whose objects are determined as garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, and which therefore consists essentially of the determination of pleasure, pain, and delusion—is, in brief, the object of experience for the Spirit (*puruṣa*). This is because it alone is the direct object of experience. External objects, however, are called objects of experience only indirectly, insofar as they are the means to that [intellectual experience]. For indeed, an object of experience is that which is presided over by the mind (*citta*).
The group of sense organs presents objects as the domain of cognition (*vidyā*).
Then, the *puruṣa* perceives the object determined by the intellect (*buddhi*), which is preceded by the self-reflective awareness (*ātma-parāmarśa*) that is a function of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
As they say: "The object determined by the intellect... (see previous note, page 78, second footnote).

"The Puruṣa cognizes. The utility of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties lies in their capacity to present objects that are either proximate or remote, but not in their capacity to produce consciousness itself. That which discriminates the presented object—along with the distinctions of the intellect, ego, and the senses—is "knowledge" (*vidyā*); this is the accomplishment of knowledge. Consequently, for the experiencing and synthesizing Puruṣa, [this occurs] within the object of experience known as the intellect.

Experience (*bhoga*) should be understood as the manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*) arising from awareness (*savid*), which takes the form of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of pleasure and so forth, and is colored by the object of enjoyment (*bhogyoparakta*), appearing as "I am happy" or "I am suffering. As it is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "The experience of this person (*puṃs*) is sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and the like. Furthermore, the intellect (*buddhi*), which is divided into the distinctions of determination, memory, intuition (*pratibhā*), and cognition (*pratyaya*), is also [the locus of experience] through which [this occurs].
That by which one discerns is knowledge (*vidyā*); and that has been called the supreme instrument (*karaṇa*). || 13 ||

Now, one might object: since cognition itself has the nature of illumination, like the sun and other luminaries, it will illuminate objects through its own determinative function (adhyavasāya) and will also cause itself to be grasped; so what is the need for another instrument called "knowledge" (vidyā)? To this, he says:
"Even if it is great and has the nature of illumination like the sun, nevertheless, because it is an object..."
That which is dependent on other instruments is incapable of making itself known. || 14 ||

Even though cognition is of the nature of light, it is not capable of making itself—which has become an object of apprehension—known as an instrument, because, like a jar or other objects, it is external insofar as it possesses the status of being an object of apprehension. This is the underlying intention here: even luminous entities such as the sun do not make themselves known by themselves alone, but rather only in dependence upon the eyes and other instruments. Therefore, even that which consists of memory and so forth...

Cognition does not apprehend itself independently, but rather only in dependence upon another instrument; thus, the establishment of *vidyā* [as such an instrument] follows from its being that very instrument. || 14 ||

But surely, it is nature (prakṛti) alone that, having transformed itself into the form of the intellect (buddhi), presents itself as an object of enjoyment for the person (puruṣa); and since the person possesses no agency but only the status of a witness, he has no requirement for instruments because of his lack of agency—thus, once again, knowledge is purposeless. To this, he says:

Due to its connection with the instruments and so forth, due to the soul's impelling them through the desire for experience, and due to its association with the fruits of their activity—that agency of the person is fully established. (15)

The agency of the *puruṣa* is established through its connection with the instruments—the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the objects [of perception] are also included. This is because the *puruṣa* acts as the impeller of those instruments and so on due to its desire for experience, and because it is joined with the fruit—pleasure and the like—of that activity consisting of the grasping of objects, which is their movement. In the reading *bhogyautsukyena*, [the meaning is the same].

This should be explained as being by means of a desire directed toward objects of enjoyment. And the underlying intention here is this: because primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is insentient, activity toward the *puruṣa* in an ultimate sense is not logical; rather, it is only for the *puruṣa*, due to his sentience, that the status of being an instigator of the instruments and so forth is possible. Therefore, agency belongs to him alone, [and] not to the non-agent.

This is because a relationship with an instrument and so forth would be purposeless. Nor can it be argued that even an insentient substance like milk is seen to act for the sake of the growth of the calf and so on from the cow; as the Sāṃkhyas have said: "Just as the activity of insentient milk is for the sake of the growth of the calf, so too is the activity of Pradhāna for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 57).
This must be said: since even milk is observed to proceed only when it is impelled by a cow or other such [cause], it is not tenable that the Pradhāna proceeds by itself. || 15 ||
Furthermore, if its status as an agent were admitted—then the designation of it as an enjoyer would be redundant, and consequently, your doctrine of the activity of *pradhāna* would be useless.
For enjoyment is not observed here to be purposeless in a person who is devoid of agency. (16)

Since experience is not observed in a person who is devoid of agency or for whom the instruments of action are not operative, it follows that experience—which is essentially of the nature of consciousness—is an action; thus, the agency of the experiencer does not cease. Consequently, if you do not admit this, your assertion of the Puruṣa’s status as an experiencer and your postulation of the activity of the insentient Pradhāna for the sake of that experience [would be untenable].

The meaning is that [the soul's agency] is not tenable because it would be purposeless. Therefore, since the person (*pums*) is the employer of the instruments and so forth, and is the enjoyer, its status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is indeed established. As they say: "He who is the lord over the causal factors (*kāraka*) in both engagement and withdrawal—whether he himself is inactive or active—he is truly called the 'agent'. (Note: The source for this citation is not found; see Maṇiprabhā on Viṣṇupurāṇa, p. 171, note 10.)
The agent. Thus [ends the section]. 16.
Thus, it has been established that agency, like the state of being a knower, is the very nature of the person (puruṣa).

Now, since these two are veiled by beginningless impurity (anādimala), they do not manifest everywhere and at all times as they do for Śiva; therefore, [the author] states that their manifestation must be brought about by something else:
Therefore, agency is that which is to be manifested, because it pertains to all objects and arises only occasionally;
like the state of being a knower, it is here to be known, and *kalā* is that which manifests it. (17)

Regarding the phrase "just as the state of being a knower": here, just like the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*)—because it does not have all things as its object and because it arises only occasionally—is perceived by some as being manifested (*vyaṅgya*) by something adventitious. Consequently, he states that the principle of *kalā* is established as the manifestor of that [agency]: "The object of knowledge is its manifestation. This refers to that [agency] which, through the partial destruction of impurity (*mala*), [is manifested].
It is the manifestor; that is the "digit" (kalā), and thus it is the accomplishment of the digit. || 17 ||

Now, one might object: even when obstructed by impurity (*mala*), the power (*śakti*) of the individual soul remains awakened by the power of Śiva at the time of creation; so what is the purpose of the category called *kalā*? To this he says:
"For without the fetter (*pāśa*), the Lord does not manifest [the power], since that [manifestation] is not universal."
A disorderly humor, even without wholesome food, does not possess the power to produce disease. || 18 ||

Since, during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the person—which consists of vision and action—is not observed to have all things as its object, therefore the Lord manifests it only by means of the fetters (*pāśa*), and not directly. However, when the impurity (*mala*) has reached maturity, He causes that [consciousness] to shine forth with all things as its object through His own power called initiation (*dīkṣā*); this we shall explain later. And therefore:

The meaning is that Śiva-Śakti bestows experience upon souls only by presiding over other principles (tattvas), not directly; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the intellect (buddhi) and the other faculties becoming useless. He confirms this very point by presenting the following analogy: "Just as a disorder (doṣa), such as wind (vāta) or bile (pitta), which has become aggravated (viṣama) and imbalanced, [cannot produce] disease without unwholesome food (apathya)."

The potter does not manifest the power of agency—the capacity to produce happiness—except through the intervention of unwholesome practice (*apathyasevā*); likewise, the Lord (*īśvara*) manifests the consciousness of souls as non-omniscient only through the intervention of bonds (*pāśa*). It is on this basis alone that he serves as an illustration here, and not because of total similarity, for [the potter] is solely a cause of suffering, whereas the Lord is not.

And this is because [the Lord] acts solely for the sake of assisting that [individual soul]. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Kiraṇa-tantra* that this agency of the Lord over the effects such as the *kalās* occurs through the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Ananta and others: "Śiva is declared to be the agent on the pure path (*śuddha-adhvan*), while Ananta is the lord on the dark path (*asita*). (Vi. 3.27). || 18 ||
Now, since enjoyment is dependent upon karma, and because it is not observed that one who is isolated in consciousness (*vijñānakevalin*)— who is devoid of karma—
experiences the perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth, [the opponent might argue] that the Lord draws forth the activity of the self's consciousness by means of karma alone. To this, he says:

Furthermore, since karma does not fulfill its purpose merely through the production of experience, [if liberation occurred then], it would follow that even knowledge [is unnecessary]; consequently, the bondage of ignorance and so forth would be rendered useless. (19)

In this case, the manifestation of the self's consciousness does not occur through action alone, because action has fulfilled its purpose solely in the production of its own fruit, and because there is no evidence for it being the cause of any other effect. Furthermore, if it were admitted that action itself is the cause of another effect, it would follow that it must also be the cause of effects such as the apprehension and determination of objects. And consequently—

There would also follow the consequence of the uselessness of principles such as *vidyā* and *buddhi*. Therefore, since it is only action (*karman*) when conjoined with other principles that serves as the cause for experience, just as *buddhi* and the others are postulated because the effects such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) cannot otherwise be accounted for, so too is *kalā* established because the manifestation of the powers of knowledge and action in the person (*puruṣa*) cannot otherwise be accounted for; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. || 19 ||
Here, an objection is raised: "Because of the prior connection with the *kalās* and so forth, vision and action do not exist [in the soul], since they are not perceived;
for in that state, devoid of a manifestor, they are simply not grasped, certainly not because of their non-existence. (20)

Since the emergence of knowledge (*jñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*) occurs only in connection with the principles beginning with *kalā*, and since these two are not observed prior to that [connection], knowledge and agency do not exist at that time as the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that Self; rather, they arise only through conjunction with *kalā* and the other principles. Therefore, it is established that the Self is merely the substratum of cognition and so forth, and not that its nature consists of knowledge and the like; such is the prima facie view.

The position [of the opponent] is as follows. But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "devoid of a manifestor" (*vyañjakarahita*). This is the intended meaning: because, like a jar or other insentient objects, there is an absence of inherence (*samavāya*) with knowledge; and because, if one were to admit the inherence of non-eternal knowledge, it would follow that [the self] too is non-eternal due to its connection with modification; and because, when a manifestor is present, the knower-form, which is the apprehending self—

Furthermore, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the nature of the Self as consisting of consciousness must be accepted as eternal. It has been stated that this essential nature of the Self does not manifest without a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) due to being veiled by beginningless impurities. Consequently, prior to the connection with *kalā* and the other categories, those two—knowledge and agency—do not manifest in that Self because they lack a manifestor, not because of their non-existence.

For non-perception caused by the absence of a manifestor does not prove non-existence; rather, it is because even when a manifestor is present—such as in the case of buried treasures and the like—there is non-perception due to the proximity of a manifestor. || 20 ||
He says this very thing:
"In the world, even when there is a perceiver, that which is not perceived is non-existent;
and likewise, cognition and action are never non-existent. (21)
For when a jar or similar object is not perceived despite the presence of a manifesting agent such as a lamp, its non-existence alone is established,

and not that of another object which is simply not perceived due to being concealed by darkness and so forth. Therefore, even the two activities of cognition and action [are absent] solely due to the absence of a manifesting agent.
"O King, these two are not perceived; therefore, they never fall into non-existence," he says: "Cognition and action. Now, one might object:

"Since prior to birth there is no certainty regarding the existence of cognition and so forth in the experiencer, doubt alone would be appropriate. This is not so; for even in infants born on that very day, specific activities such as drinking, walking, or striking are preceded by effort.

Since [the capacity for] cognition and agency are established at the time of empirical activity through their invariable concomitance with the recollection of what is beneficial and harmful, their existence prior to birth is indeed proven. || 21 ||
He establishes this very point by means of an illustration:

"Just as the status of being a cook is established prior to the act of cooking, so too, since the individual soul (aṇu) is established prior to cognition and its instruments, from where could its [cognitive] power arise? (22)

Just as, by observing the act of cooking, it is understood that the capacity for cooking—which was already present at a prior time—is already existing in the cook even before [the action], and not that it arises only at that very moment; so too, from the observation of the effects of cognition, it is determined that the powers of the acts of cognition exist in the self even beforehand. Thus it has been said:

In the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Consciousness, whose nature is perception and action, exists in the self at all times; and because it is heard [in scripture] as being 'all-facing' (*sarvatomukha*) in liberation, it is omnipresent.
And therefore—
Because it depends upon manifesting agents, there exists at its root the obscuration of vision and action;
for in the absence of that [obscuration], since vision and action would pertain to all objects, the atom (the soul) would not undergo transmigratory existence.

Since, during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), knowledge and action are observed to depend upon manifesting factors, it is therefore determined that there exists some cause for this dependence, namely, the veiling of vision and action (dṛkkriyācchādana). It is heard [in scripture] that in the absence of which, liberated souls—possessing knowledge and agency that, like those of the Lord, have all things as their object—have no further connection with transmigratory existence. Now, one might object:

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the self (*ātman*) is inherently pure; however, this is incorrect, because its dependence on another is observed during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, if that dependence were causeless, it would follow that even one who is liberated remains dependent. Moreover, knowledge and action require a manifesting agent. As it is said: "In the absence of fetters (*pāśa*), dependence must be explained [otherwise]."
"What is its basis? (*Mṛgendravyākhyā* 7.2), and so forth. || 23 ||
He states the order of the emergence of these [principles], beginning with the Unmanifest:
"The Unmanifest, Attachment, and Ignorance arise from Kalā; and Kalā is born from Māyā.
This group of principles, beginning with Earth and ending with Kalā, is determined for each individual soul. (24)
And this [individual soul] wanders by the power of karma through all the bodies born within the worlds;
furthermore, the other "world-forms" (bhuvanākṛti) are to be understood as the constituent parts (skandha) of those [principles] ending with *kalā*. (25)

As it is stated in the *Raurava*: "From the principle of *kalā*, the two principles of *rāga* and *vidyā* came into being, as well as the *avyakta*" (*Vijñānabhairava* 2.15). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and *kalā*," both *kāla* and *niyati* are included as having arisen from *māyā*;

for this is heard in scripture that *kāla* and *niyati* also originate from *māyā* and serve as auxiliaries to the activity of experience (*bhoga*). To illustrate: in the absence of *niyati*, even [actions] acquired by others...

Others might enjoy the fruits of actions—just as bandits might enjoy the fruits of agriculture and the like performed by the twice-born and others in the absence of royal regulation; thus, *niyati* (the principle of necessity) is established as the regulator. Furthermore, *kāla* (time) is also established as the cause for regulating the duration of that very experience, being evidenced by such perceptions as "long" or "quick";
this and more has been explained by us at length in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* and the *Tattvaprakāśavṛtti*. Thus it was said:

And in the *Mṛgendra*: "Time, which arises from Māyā, is the object of cognitions such as 'a moment' (*truṭi*); it restrains the bound soul (*paśu*) through Necessity (*niyati*), impelling [him] from [the state of] non-arising. (Vi. 10.14). And these two principles have not been established in detail by the Teacher because they are external in relation to Kalā and the others; rather, they are indicated by the word "and" (*ca*), so there is no contradiction. And this...

He states that the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), consisting of the thirty principles beginning with *kalā*, is the instrument of experience for each individual soul because it is fixed to every person—beginning with "the earth and so forth. This is stated in the *Mṛgendratantra*: "From the *prayoktrī* down to the earth, this [subtle body] is the means for accomplishing the purpose of the individual soul" (Vi.
12.32). For this very reason, it is taught that during initiation (*dīkṣā*), the purification of the subtle body must be performed specifically in the lower portion of the *māyā*-tattva.
In the *Raurava* and other scriptures: "But surely it is heard in the venerable *Kālottara*: 'Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city)'? (17.4–5). True;
therefore, this sūtra has been explained by the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha as denoting thirty principles (*tattvas*). If that is so..."

How does this [individual] possess the nature of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka)? It consists of five groups known as the gross elements, the subtle elements, the organs of cognition, the organs of action, and the internal organ; its cause, the principle of the *guṇas*; that which fills it, *pradhāna*; and that which assists the nature of the enjoyer, consisting of the five-fold sheath beginning with *kalā*.

There is no contradiction because [the body] is originated by a group [of causes]. Furthermore, it should be understood that this subtle body (sūkṣma-śarīra), despite the diversity of external bodies, is one and the same for each individual from the beginning of creation until its end in dissolution, or until the attainment of liberation in the interim. Having thus described the creation of the principles (tattva) such as *kalā* and so forth, which constitute the unique form [of the subtle body], [the author now speaks] of the Self itself.

He describes the common creation consisting of the worlds, which serves as the substratum for the worlds, bodies, objects, and so forth, that arise in accordance with karma—beginning with the words: "And the forms of the worlds... (verses 24–25).

And since these principles (tattvas), being fixed for each individual soul, are insentient, manifold, and possess parts by virtue of being the substratum of the worlds, their status as effects is established; therefore, it is said that Māyā, their material cause, is proven:
"Beyond the modified [evolutes] is Māyā, which is eternal, all-pervasive, insentient, and one."
She is the support and the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world. || 26 ||

Because it is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of creation and so forth, it is recited as being the substratum for its own class of effects through modification; "it is recited" is the ellipsis to be supplied. And that [nature] is eternal, because it is the ultimate cause, and because if one were to admit a further material cause for it, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). It is also all-pervasive (*vibhvī*), encompassing its own effects.
Furthermore, it is insentient precisely because it is a material cause (*upādāna*); for it is observed that material causes such as clay and the like are indeed insentient.

Moreover, it is one precisely because it is the ultimate cause (*paramakāraṇa*). For if there were multiplicity while remaining insentient, then—due to that multiplicity—a further cause would have to be sought, as in the case of jars and other objects, and from that a regressus ad infinitum (*anavasthā*) would result. For this very reason, it has been stated that atoms are not the ultimate cause. Now, [one might object]: [The objection follows: "But..."

The knowers of the Vedānta maintain that the Supreme Self alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world; this is incorrect. For if it were the material cause, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), just like clay and other such substances. Furthermore, if it were the cause of both the sentient and the insentient, it too would possess that dual nature, and by virtue of having parts (*sāṃśatva*), it would follow that it is itself an effect. This is because: "When entities possess a certain form, they are produced from a cause of that same form. And this...

This refutation should also be understood to apply to the "supreme nature" (paraprakṛti) known as Nārāyaṇa, which is accepted by the Pāñcarātras, because the logic is the same. Here, by the phrase "the substratum of creation, maintenance, and dissolution," [the author] demonstrates that, according to the view of the Satkāryavāda, at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), the effects such as the *kalās* remain in a subtle form within *māyā*. As it is heard in scripture:

"In the state of withdrawal, the effects, which exist in the form of power (*śakti*), have that [cause] as their support; in the state of manifestation, they function in the form of manifest entities for the accomplishment of the purpose.
(Mṛgendra-vṛtti 9.13). Furthermore, this doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been established by us in detail in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*. (26)

Having thus established the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), he describes that [principle] for whose benefit this [path] exists: "The reality (*tattva*) which is eternal and all-pervading, yet whose power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) has been obstructed by impurity (*mala*) from time immemorial, is designated as the 'bound soul' (*paśu*). Indeed, this [pure path] is declared to be its equipment (*parikara*) for the sake of experience (*bhoga*). (27)

That which has been described as the illusory (*māyīya*) equipment—consisting of both common and uncommon forms—for the sake of experiencing karma, is called the *paśu* (bound soul) principle because its knowledge and action are obscured from beginningless time by the impurity (*mala*) known as *paśutva* (the state of being a bound soul). For this very reason, impurity is not a separate ontological principle (*tattvāntara*), but is rather included within the *paśu* principle itself; for without it, the state of being a bound soul would be impossible.
That reality is eternal, and not momentary as for the Buddhists, because we observe the recollection of what was previously experienced;

furthermore, if it were momentary, the performance of action and the enjoyment of its fruit would be untenable. Moreover, it is all-pervading, and not limited to the body like that of the Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas), nor subject to the properties of contraction and expansion.

Because such [a single Self] would entail defects such as insentience and impermanence, and because we observe a variety of experiences due to the fact that [beings] are the enjoyers of the fruits of their actions, the plurality of selves is established by the very nature of things. This will also be stated at the time of refuting transmigration (*saṃkrānti*). In this regard, when there is a desire for liberation from the beginningless connection with both the immutable, eternal *mala* and the eternally flowing *karman*, [The text continues: ...[omitted]... [the Lord] acts. Thus, the plurality of selves is proven. Furthermore, it is not the case that the Lord acts toward one self while another remains indifferent; rather, He acts toward all simultaneously. For if He were to act toward some and not others, He would be subject to partiality (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*), which would contradict His nature as the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the Lord acts toward all selves simultaneously. Consequently, the plurality of selves is established.
