Śambhu, for the sake of ripening impurity (*mala*) and for the experiencing of karma, effects a connection with the *māyīya* [principles] beginning with *kalā*;

at that time, this Self is called *sakala*. However, during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), due to the withdrawal of *kalā* and the other principles, it is joined with impurity and karma and is thus called *pralayākala*. Through the destruction of karma by means of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*) and yoga, etc., it remains joined with impurity alone and is called *vijñānakala*.
These and other such divisions of the bound soul (paśu) have been demonstrated by us in detail in our commentary on the *Tattvaprakāśa*. || 27 ||
And this [is the case]:

the path of the principles (tattvas), beginning from the bottom, has its web of bonds destroyed by the power of Śiva known as initiation and knowledge; and the individual soul (aṇu) has its vision and action manifested. || 28 ||

For in that context, *dīkṣā* is defined as the activity of Śiva’s power (*śakti*) directed toward the object of grace, whether performed by a teacher or independent of one. Consequently, the individual soul (*aṇu*), whose net of bonds such as impurity has been removed by Śiva’s power and whose knowledge and action regarding all objects have thus been manifested, comes to be designated as the "Pure Path" (*śuddhādhvan*). As it is said in the *Raurava*:

"Free from all impurities, situated in the digit of Śiva and Śakti, this pure reality of the Self (ātmatattva)" (Viṣṇusaṃhitā 4.43). Now, it may be argued that liberation for the selves occurs through knowledge alone, as held by the Vedāntins, Sāṃkhyas, and others; however, that is incorrect. Since impurity (*mala*) is a substance, its removal cannot occur through knowledge alone—just as a cataract on the eye cannot be removed by mere knowledge—but rather [requires something else].

It is by the very operation of the Lord known as initiation (dīkṣā), just like the operation of an oculist; for it is stated in the *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "Initiation alone liberates and leads one upward even to the abode of Śiva. (28)

And this designation applies only to his conjunction with a body, which is based on his authority (*adhikāra*) and so forth following his reception of grace (*anugraha*), and not to the attainment of supreme liberation in the form of equality with Śiva; for at that time, he is designated precisely as a "liberated Śiva" (*muktaśiva*).
Thus it is said: "He beholds Śiva through his own power and meditates upon Him with a vision illumined by Śiva."
He worships Śambhu with mantras for the benefit of himself and others. || 29 ||

This pure Self, by means of its own power consisting of the capacity for Śiva, meditates upon and perceives Śiva through that vision. As it is stated in the *Mokṣakārikā*: "By means of the vision of consciousness empowered by the rays of the power of the sun that is Śiva, the Self, with its veils removed, perceives Śiva together with [His] powers and other attributes. (Śloka 111) Therefore, unlike what is taught in the Pātañjala and other systems...
It has been stated that it is not possible for Śiva to be an object of cognition and so forth, because He is beyond the reach of the fetters (*pāśa*).

As it is said in that very same work: "The modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) known as 'awareness' (*bodha*) is not capable of manifesting the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), because [that awareness] is itself a fetter, like shackles and the like. (Śloka 106) Furthermore, He [acts] for the sake of benefiting both Himself and others.

He worships that very [Lord] with various sacrifices. As it is said in the *Raurava*: "Those proficient in mantras and tantras, authorized by the guru and the tantra, and whose bonds have been severed by initiation, worship with various sacrifices" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 2.21–22). In this regard, the teachers (*ācāryas*), the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*), and others, for the sake of their own benefit upon the exhaustion of their office, and for the sake of benefiting others through the granting of enjoyment and liberation, [perform these rites].

The distinction is that [the officiants] sacrifice for their own sake, while the practitioner (sādhaka) or the spiritual son (putraka) sacrifices for the sake of their own enjoyment and liberation. || 29 ||
Among them, he describes the principle of the Lord who presides over Māyāgarbha:

"Śrīkaṇṭha, the Maṇḍalins, Krodha and the others, the hundred Bhavas, and the Vīreśas—these have their vision and action manifested by the Supreme Lord through the conjunction with Kalā and the other [principles]. (30)

In that regard, there are eight Maṇḍalins situated at the summit of the *kalā*-tattva. As it is stated in the Raurava: "The path of reality (*tattvamārga*) which is established for the lords of the maṇḍalas... (Viṣṇusaṃhitā 4.21). Śrīkaṇṭha is the abode of the *guṇa*-tattva and the creator of the worlds and regions below; and the eight [lords] beginning with Krodha, who reside at the summit of the *guṇa*-tattva, are the hundred-fold beings, the hundred Rudras.

They are the sustainers of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Vīreśa, Vīrabhadra, and the presiding lord of the hundred Rudras—these have had their vision and action manifested by Śiva alone. Consequently, despite being bound by the *ari* (the six enemies) and being joined with the *kalās* and so forth, they do not possess perverted knowledge like bound souls (*paśu*), because they are directly favored by Śiva. As it has been said: "Even when joined with the *kalās*, they are not subject to them like the multitude of bound souls."

(Mo. Kā. 82). However, that connection with *kalā* and the other categories is performed by Ananta alone, according to the scriptural statement: "In the pure path, Śiva is said to be the agent; in the impure [path], Ananta is the Lord" (Ki. Vi. 3.27). || 30 ||
They bring about enjoyment and liberation for men within their own domain by necessity.
And he says that this other reality is the Mantreśvara-tattva, which holds authority over the interior of Māyā:
"This Mantreśa-tattva is supreme, possessing authority over the effects of Māyā. (31)

Having thus spoken of the Supreme Lord of Mantras, he says the following in order to explain the mantras: "At the beginning of creation, millions of atoms, their veils pierced by the Lord, have their powers of vision and agency ignited; this indeed is the reality known as 'mantra'. (32)
And here, according to the scriptural statement, "He awakened eight individuals who were *vijñānakevalas*" (*Mālinīvijayottara* 1.19),

and because they abide on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), it is only those among the *vijñānakalas* whose impurities have reached full maturity who are appointed to the status of *vidyeśvara* or *mantreśvara*, by virtue of the varying degrees of that maturation.

It should be understood that [this state] exists only for the *pralayākalas*, who possess unripened impurities (*apakvamala*) and reside on the path of impurity (*aśuddhādhvan*), because they lack the status of being supreme lords of the mantras (*aparamantreśvaratva*).

Regarding the word "mantra" here, one should consult the *Sārdhatriśatikālottaravṛtti* (p. 4, note 22). This verse is also found in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* (Kriyāpāda 1.1): "Mantra is the capacity for all-knowingness (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), which is the bestowing of grace upon those transmigrating beings."

"Because they possess the nature of protecting through reflection (*manana*), they are called *mantras*," according to this scriptural statement (*śruti*). Thus, [the term] applies to Śiva, Śakti, and those who are graced by them.

However, we shall explain that the status of being a *mantra* belongs to expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*) only figuratively (*upacārāt*). Furthermore, because they are stainless, their knowledge and action are manifested;

because they are endowed with the attributes of reflection and so forth, and because they reside within the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā-tattva*), they are described as such in the Śaiva scriptures such as the *Raurava*.
These are called the reality of mantra (mantratattva).

For this very reason, the teachers maintain that prior to the conjunction with Śuddhavidyā, the severance of impurity (malavicchitti) must be effected during initiation while [the soul] is still in the upper station. || 32 ||
Now he states their function as bestowers of grace:
"In this world, half of the mantras brought forth by Śiva go toward men who have been graced, proceeding without the form of a teacher when employed by the Lord. (33)

Among those atoms numbering seven crores, half of them—without depending on any heavy substratum—is impelled by Īśvara; having favored the persons who have been brought together by Śiva and made objects of His grace through the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*), it departs immediately after creation. The word "grace" (*anugraham*) is to be supplied as the object. As it has been said:

In the *Mṛgendra*: "Having performed its office throughout the entire path, depending upon the body of the agent, it enters Śiva—who is accompanied by the Lord—at the end of [Śiva's] persistence. Below that, without an office, another [power] belonging to the Lord, having performed its office over the primary transformation, departs" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 4.7–8). Among those [souls], those possessing a specific ripening of impurity attain liberation immediately after creation; others [do not].
The meaning is: "only at the time of reabsorption. || 33 ||
For this very reason, he describes the function of the other half:
"The other [half] is joined with the maṇḍala-mantras created by Śiva and is employed by the Lord through the practice known as initiation (dīkṣā), which resides within the body of the teacher. (34)
Like poison, it suddenly cuts away the impurities, karmic tendencies, sources of birth, and their effects for the bound soul;
yet, when propitiated, it bestows various supernatural powers upon the foremost of practitioners.

Accompanied by the great maṇḍalas, such as the vidyāṅga-maṇḍala, which were produced by Śiva for the sake of favoring bound souls (paśus), and by the mantras heard as being worthy of worship therein, another half [of the ritual]— when employed by Īśvara abiding in the form of the Ācārya—
suddenly cuts away the impurities, karmas, and effects of māyā of the bound soul, just like poison. For this very reason, it belongs to the sakala [level] alone.

The grace of Śiva is mediated through the Guru, because that [grace] alone effects the removal of the three bonds. Here, *mala* is singular, yet it possesses multiple powers that obscure the various individual souls; it is eternal and all-pervasive. As it is stated:
"That one [impurity] of all beings is beginningless, dense, and great; residing within each soul, it consists of a multitude of powers that perish at the end of their own time. (Mṛgendra)

(Vi. 7.8). Consequently, since it is the ripening of that very power [of *mala*] which is obstructed by initiation (*dīkṣā*), the objection that all would be liberated simultaneously if *mala* were a single entity is also avoided. Furthermore, *karman*—consisting of merit and demerit—is restricted to the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and is beginningless by way of a continuous flow (*pravāha*). *Yoni*, however, is *māyā*, along with its effects, which take both common and uncommon forms.

Because they have karma as their cause, even though these [impurities] are adventitious, they are indeed beginningless in their continuity, since the succession of karma and body is established as being beginningless, like the seed and the sprout. And these impurities, such as *mala* and the rest,
are removed by the activity of the Lord through the instrumentality of mantra known as *dīkṣā*, just as the removal of poison is observed to occur through an action preceded by mantra.

Therefore, the difference is this: mantras function as auxiliary instruments (*anugrāhakakaraṇa*), whereas the Vidyeśvaras—who are both supreme and subordinate—act as the actual agents (*kartṛ*) like the Teacher (*ācārya*). Furthermore, when propitiated for this purpose, [the mantra] bestows various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) upon practitioners who desire worldly enjoyments. As it is said in the Raurava: "This statement is not found in the Raurava" (this is the reading in the manuscript).
(See commentary on page 26, note 7)—
Those purified by initiation, born within the maṇḍala of Gaṇapati and the Guru,
are perfected beings (*siddhas*) whose bodies shine with the splendor of the orb of the rising sun through the mantras.

Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time, accompanied by hosts of celestial women, their longing subsided, they become partakers of the supreme sovereignty of the auspicious state. Thus [ends verse 35].
But how is it known that the cessation of bondage has occurred for the self through initiation (*dīkṣā*)? To this he says:

"One should know from the sign (*pratyaya*)—namely, that [the soul] attains purity in the balance (*tulā*) due to initiation by the Supreme Lord—that there is the removal of bondage, just like the destruction of poison. (36)

In this context, it is observed that even one who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) becomes free from sin through initiation. For instance, as stated in the venerable *Kālottara* and other scriptures, after testing his worthiness by means of placing him upon the balance (dhaṭāropaṇa) obtained through the mantra,
and subsequently performing his purification preceded by the utterance of the *udghāta-mantra* and so forth, when he is placed upon the balance once again— his [weight]...
Lightness is observed arising [in the body]. This is an illustration of other causal conditions (pratyaya), such as the rendering [of the body] seedless (nirbījakaraṇa) and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that from this observed causal condition, just as poison is removed by the action of a snake-charmer, the removal of bondage is accomplished through the rite known as initiation (dīkṣā). And for that very reason, in matters of perceived objects...

Having observed that the scriptures concerning poisons, elemental spirits, alchemy, and so forth, are effective in their results, one infers that the truth of that scripture—though its results are not yet perceived—is likewise real; thus, Śiva’s status as the supreme authority (*paramāpta*) is established. As it is said in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* (on *Vidyāpāda* 1.1): "From the fact that [the scriptures on] poisons and the like are seen to be free from error, and from the efficacy of mantras accompanied by their proper phonetic forms..."
"Because he has been obtained through the grand display of the Rasopaniṣad, he is accepted. Thus [ends verse 36].
If this were so, then because all sins are destroyed by initiation alone, it would follow that the body would fall at that very moment; therefore, he says:
"The physical body does not fall for one who has merely been initiated, because of the burning away of the karma that produces future results."
And there is a certain initiation which even destroys the fruit that is currently ripening. || 37 ||

Because only those karmas whose fruits are yet to come are consumed by the initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), and because the body persists after initiation due to the presence of karma that has already begun its effect (*ārabdhakārya*), the maintenance of the body subsequent to initiation is not contradictory. As it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "Karma spanning many lifetimes has been burnt by the individual souls like a seed; indeed, it is that [initiation] by which even future [karma] is obstructed."

"Through enjoyment" (Vi. 6.19). But when impurity has reached ultimate maturity, even that [residual karma] is destroyed by means of the *sadyonirvāṇa* initiation; thus he says, "And it comes to pass. Even in that case, a continued existence for some time is indeed possible due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). As they say: "He remains with his body sustained by the force of residual impressions, like the whirling of a potter's wheel" (Sāṃkhya Kārikā 67). || 37 ||
Now, he specifies what was stated by the *Jñāpaka* regarding that which, though yet to come, is also obstructed:

"Even an action performed would not lead to its fruit—like a seed sown in barren soil after initiation—unless one abandons that single act born from the conflict with a more powerful, specific scripture. (38)

Ritual action consisting of *iṣṭāpūrta* and so forth, which is performed because it is prescribed for the period subsequent to initiation (*dīkṣā*), has its power obstructed by that very initiation and thus does not produce fruits such as union with a body. However, ritual action such as the propitiation of mantras, which is established by specific scriptures and performed by the practitioner, is indeed productive of fruit. As it has been said:

In the *Sūkṣmasvāyambhuva*: "Whoever should desire enjoyments in a particular [world], he is joined to that very place through the power of the mantra; thus he becomes a possessor of supernatural powers (*siddhi*). Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that even for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), if they fail to perform what is enjoined by the specific scriptures or perform what is prohibited by them, and have not performed expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is the occurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*): "Because of the transgression of the rules (*samaya*)."

The reading found there is: "For transgressing the command, the state of being a flesh-eater is declared for a hundred years" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 25.2). And because it is enjoined by that [scripture], the conduct pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*), even though established by general scriptures, must indeed be performed.
As it is heard—[this is recorded] as the word of the venerable Bhārgava in the *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā* (Vi 1.1)—so it is remembered.

"One should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in one's mind. Whoever, while remaining in a particular stage of life, has received initiation whose essence is Śiva, he, remaining steadfast in that very stage, should protect the Dharma of Śiva. (38)
Now, one might ask: for one who has incurred the transgression of violating the rules (*samaya*) and has not yet performed the penance, is there liberation or not? To this, he says:
"Therefore, even though he has not performed the rite, for some time he becomes a king among the excellent Piśācas."
Indeed, through delusion, this stainless self attains equality with the Supreme Lord. || 39 ||

And here, after initiation, the destruction of the bonds (*pāśa*) of the commenced task is brought about through the daily diminution of the performance of the rules (*samaya*), such as bathing and worship. Therefore, those capable who have received initiation with expectations (*sāpekṣa-dīkṣā*) must perform the specific conduct of the rules (*samayācāra-viśeṣa*); and for the ignorant who have received initiation without expectations (*nirapekṣa-dīkṣā*).

Service to the Guru, worship of Śiva, and so forth, should be performed as much as possible; for it is precisely through the performance of these that the completion of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is inferred. Consequently, for one whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is most intense by virtue of the ripening of their impurity (*mala*), there is no deficiency in initiation nor any transgression of the rules (*samaya*); such a person attains liberation immediately upon the fall of the body. But for one who...

Due to the dullness resulting from the ripening of impurities, for one whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is extremely weak and so forth, a transgression of the rules (*samayollaṅghana*) may occur by chance through divine or human opposition after initiation. Such a person, having failed to observe the conduct of the rules and not having performed the rite of expiation, experiences the fruit of the transgression—which consists of becoming a king of the *piśācas*—just like the fruit of a worldly desire; thereafter, his soul becomes pure once again.

One attains liberation, which consists of equality with Paraśiva. As it has been said: "The intellect of one who is purified by expiation is proclaimed to be pure. However, for one who has received initiation through artificial devotion to a guru and the like for worldly purposes, and who intentionally fails to observe the rules of conduct (*samaya*), that purity is not achieved; rather, the guru becomes subject to expiation. As it is heard in that regard: [text follows].

"One who applies himself falsely, whether a minor or a teacher, shall undergo penance" (Mṛgendra-kriyā-pāda 8.242), and "The teacher, having been initiated, should perform the initiation of the self for one who has strayed. || 39 ||

Having thus established the fruit of the incidental initiation (*prāsaṅgikadīkṣā*), he now states, in the present context following the [discussion of] mantras, who the Lords of Mantra (*mantreśvara*) are: "Prior to the creation of the mantras and so forth, eight individual souls (*aṇu*) were released from their coverings by the Lord; they have been endowed with the capacity for the operation of knowledge regarding all objects. (40)

Even prior to the creation of the mantras and other categories, eight *aṇus*—known as the *vijñānakalas*—had their impurities removed by Śiva and were endowed with the knowledge and capacity for action regarding all objects. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:

"Therein, at the outset, He creates for the qualified *aṇus* alone a group of eight, joined with the powers beginning with Vāmā and surrounded by the seventy million [mantras]. (Vi. 4.2) Thus ends [verse] 40.
Who are they, and what do they do? To this he says:
"Those, headed by Ananteśa, impel the mantras and others due to their status as Lords (pati).
Impelled by the will of Hara, they perform creation, maintenance, dissolution, and liberation. (41)

And they—known by the names Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin—as Mantramaheśvaras impel the mantras and other [principles]. Furthermore, they perform the fourfold [cosmic] process beginning with emission (sarga), which is inseparable from that [emanation], as well as enjoyment (bhoga) and concealment (tirobhāva). As it is said in the Raurava:

"Performing the maintenance, protection, bestowal, manifestation, and grace [of the universe]" (Vijñānabhairava 1.15). Although they possess authority over these five functions, he states that they do not possess equality with Śiva: "impelled by the will of Hara. Because they are impelled through their connection to the dissolution of their office (*adhikāra-mala*), their agency is inferior to that of Śiva by a degree (*kalā*); the agency of the Mantras and Mantreśvaras is even more inferior than theirs. For this very reason, [the case] of Ananta...

Their supreme excellence is heard [in scripture]: "Of those of infinite power, Ananta is the Supreme Lord" (Rauravaviveka 2.12). However, omniscience is common to all of them, as no distinction is heard [regarding this]. And it is stated in the Raurava and other texts that for all of these, liberation occurs at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) due to the cessation of their office: "Ananta is the highest among those great ones..."
"For the universal monarchs, the supreme state has been established as the cause of all-creatorship. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.13) || 41 ||
Thus, those who rely on the principle of Īśvara are called Mantreśvaras; regarding this, he says:
"This is the principle of the Mantreśas: the *paramāṇus* and their lords in the two paths.
For the designator follows the designated, since for us a designation is not without meaning. (42)

In the two paths (*adhvan*) which consist of both the pure and the impure, the *aṇus* who possess the yoga of reflection and protection, as well as their lords—the Mantreśvaras and Mantramaheśvaras—are so designated. By this, he demonstrates that there also exist *mantras* with impurities (*sāñjana*) residing in the impure path. As it has been said—(see the commentary on the Sārdhatriśatikālottara, p. 146, note 7)—others...

"The mantras of Pradhāna are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others who are higher; they possess *añjana* (ointment/manifestation), reside within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), and consist of the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Therefore, since expressive words are insentient, the properties of "thinking" (*manana*) and "protecting" (*trāṇa*) are impossible for them; he states that they are designated by the term "mantra" only figuratively, by virtue of being denoters [of the mantras].
Regarding the term "denotative" (*abhidhāyaka*): words that denote objects such as "pot" or "cloth" are observed to be grounded solely in the denoted object (*vācyārtha*).

Therefore, by means of mantras consisting of words that denote [entities] such as Ananta and the rest—which function as *liṅga*s—those who are denoted, namely the selves of Mantreśvara and the others, are established as the bestowers of fruits through the recitation (*japa*) and other practices of those mantras. By this, it is shown that the deity is indeed nothing but the word itself.
Those Mīmāṃsakas who hold such views have been refuted, because that which is insentient produces an effect only through the superintendence of a sentient being.

Therefore, it should be understood that, just as in the case of an image and so forth, it is the mantras denoting Śiva and others that, when manifested within the sound consisting of the mantra, bestow the fruit. || 42 ||

And here, since sound possesses a specific arrangement and is therefore an effect—just like a jar—and since it is impossible for the relationship between a word and its meaning to be eternal (given these conditions), that relationship must be conventional; thus, he states that the omniscient Lord alone is the creator of that convention:
"Śambhu [is the master] of the Vidyās and Vidyeśas, through his knowledge of both general and particular properties."
For it is observed that one who knows the meaning is the creator of designations for mantras. || 43 ||

Since in the world it is observed that only the father or others—who know the specific purpose of things such as sons—act as the designators of those things, therefore Śambhu alone created the mantras which are the designators of the Mantreśvara-selves; for he alone is the knower of their general and specific characteristics. Their general characteristic consists of eternality, pervasiveness, and so forth.

However, the specific characteristic [of Mahāmāyā] should be understood as the state of being the material cause for the application of various levels (*pada*) according to the remaining impurities (*mala*). In this context,

because she is the material cause of the words consisting of mantras and so forth, and because she is the material cause of the worlds (*bhuvana*) of the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*) which serve as the substratum for the bodies and senses of the Vidyeśvaras and others, she is known as Kuṇḍalinī Mahāmāyā.

It is established. As it is stated in the *Raurava* and other scriptures: "Above Māyā is Mahāmāyā" (*Viṣamapada* 4.28). Also in the *Mṛgendra*: "From Śakti arises Nāda, then Bindu, the Imperishable, and from that the Mātṛkā" (*Kriyāpāda* 1.2), and likewise in the context of the Pure Path: "Of the supreme Māyā" (*Mṛgendravṛtti* 13.5). And this differentiation of the pure principles, such as Vedya, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, is the Supreme Bindu which serves as their cause.

The various modes of accomplishment have been explained in detail in the *Mataṅga* and other scriptures, and we ourselves have established them in the *Ratnatrayollekhinī*; therefore, they should be understood from those very sources. || 43 ||

Now, it is stated that in the Āgamas, these Vidyeśvaras and others are heard of as being of the nature of a union with Śakti and Śiva, who are differentiated by the various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) over which they respectively preside:
"The views of the wise regarding the individual soul (aṇu), Śakti, and Śambhu [apply] to the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras."
Śiva is one and changeless, and his power is likewise; therefore, those two are not [mutually] fit.
Or rather, because it would be subject to modification if it were to exist in many ways or if it were devoid of consciousness;
therefore, Śambhu alone must indeed exist as one, like a yogi, while abiding in manifold forms. (45)

In the Gītā it is heard: "The Śruti declares that Śiva is the mantra for the sake of blessing the world; that power which is the bestower of grace has here attained the state of being mantra. Furthermore: "Twenty-four supreme lords of mantras are proclaimed—the Āṇavas, the Śāmbhavas, the Śāktas, and likewise other millions of mantras. Thus, they are indeed the supports of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa)."
"Preceded by Vīrabhadra," and so forth. Among these, according to the view of the *Aṇu* (the dualist), the distinction is primary, as previously stated.
However, in the views of Śambhu and Śakti, this distinction is merely figurative (*aupacārika*) due to their presiding over [the individual soul]; thus he says: "Śiva is one.

Here, Śiva alone is the creator of the universe and the benefactor of all, because He alone is eternally liberated from the beginningless [bondage]. And it is said in the *Raurava* and other scriptures: "The Śiva-principle..."
"For there is only one Supreme" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.4). The Śruti also says: "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second" (Atharva Upaniṣad 2.7).

Furthermore, if there were multiple lords, the accomplishment of the world's effects would not be possible, because even things like chariots, which have many makers, do not arise without following the will of a single architect. As they say: "Where there are many leaders..."

"All those who consider themselves wise all desire greatness, yet that [desire] clearly perishes. By this, the position of the *pravāheśvara* (the Lord as the flowing stream) is also refuted; for since sovereignty consists in the attainment of the manifestation of one's own nature, its destruction is impossible.
Furthermore, He is changeless because of His eternity and His consciousness. His power is likewise of the same nature, because it is an attribute of Him. Indeed, not...

An eternal entity cannot be joined with impermanent attributes, because if the attribute and the substratum are non-different, it would follow that the substratum itself is impermanent. Therefore, it is logical that Śakti and Śiva exist in many ways through various divisions such as Ananta and others;
otherwise, if their manifold states were admitted, they would—due to being subject to modification—be rendered insentient like Māyā and the rest.

Furthermore, it is not logical for those two to be insentient, because they are heard of as being precisely sentient; moreover, it is impossible for that which is insentient to undergo transformation and so forth without the superintendence of a sentient being. Therefore, the distinction between the two is merely figurative. As it is said: "He is the possessor of authority, the enjoyer, and the one who merges, figuratively speaking," and likewise: "But whatever distinction of lords exists here is like the distinction of powers (*śakti*) in this scripture."

"And: 'The distinction [of the deity] arises from the distinction of the locus, through the metaphorical application of the distinction of functions' (Mṛgendravidyāpāda 13.164–165). Here, he states the objection of another: "Now, as for Śambhu... (vv. 44–45).

If it is argued that even though Śiva is one, he acquires different designations such as Sadāśiva, Ananta, and so forth by presiding over multiple bodies—as is the case with a yogi—that is incorrect; thus [the author] says:
"For his power is his form, and that is indeed one; nor is this [multiplicity] primary."
There are many persons who partake in the highest good, and among them, there is a gradation in their vision and action. || 46 ||
Therefore, the primary [manifestation] arising from that is seen through the excellence of the difference in its manifestors;

for since Śiva, by virtue of being stainless and the ultimate reality, cannot possess bodies such as those of the *bindu* and so forth, it is his Power (*śakti*) alone—which performs the functions of a body—that is metaphorically called "form" (*mūrti*). And it has been stated that this [Power] is one and the same. Consequently, even the differentiation into Īśāna and the others is not real.

Thus, even the distinction of bodies for him, as in the case of yogins, is not primary. Now, one might object: "The five-faced one, the fifteen-eyed one," and so forth—does this not show that even Śiva has a distinction of bodies? True; even that is heard only for the purpose of meditation. As stated in the Pauṣkara: "The form of Him is described for the sake of the practitioner's objective. However, the distinction regarding the atomic nature (of the self) is...

He states that [the soul] is indeed primary: "Many are those who possess the highest good. For here, due to the diversity of experiences and the diversity of births and deaths, these persons who partake in the highest good for the sake of experience and liberation are seen to be many indeed.
And because they possess manifesting bodies, sense organs, and so forth, their excellence is observed, as well as a progressive increase in knowledge and action.

Therefore, for these Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras as well, their arising and differentiation are indeed real, due to the distinctions in their respective offices and the distinctions among their worlds, according to the specific types of Śiva’s grace as previously described. || 46 ||
And therefore:
Śiva and Śakti accomplish their purpose here by mounting those [powers], due to the differentiation inherent therein. || 47 ||
They appear as if distinct by virtue of their qualities and their classes;

for it is by presiding over them that Śiva and Śakti accomplish the goals of the individual soul (puruṣārtha). Therefore, through that distinction, they too become as if distinct. And that Śiva, together with his Śakti, [is so designated] through a figurative application (gauṇyā vṛttyā) based on the connection with the various functions residing therein.
He comes to possess those respective designations. || 47 ||
Therefore, he says that Śiva alone is the benefactor of all:
"He is eternally pure by nature, omniscient, the doer of all, and the Lord. (48)
Śambhu, whose power is unimpeded, is the sole friend of all persons;
and herein, a twofold power has been declared for the sake of accomplishing awakening, meditation, and so forth. (49)
The expression "the form and that which possesses it" is a figurative statement regarding power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).

In this scripture, for the sake of attaining enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), and as objects of knowledge, two principles are taught known as the "with-parts" (*sakala*) and the "partless" (*niṣkala*), designated as power and the possessor of power. It should be understood that the description of these two—power and the possessor of power—in terms of "form" and "that which possesses form" is intended as a figurative designation.

This is what is meant: in the state of *adhikāra* (sovereign authority), his form (*mūrti*) is indeed power (*śakti*) itself, differentiated by the thirty-eight divisions of *kalās* due to the diversity of its functions. It is precisely through association with that [power] that he is called *sakala* (with parts); when joined with the cessation of activity, he is *niṣkala* (without parts). || 48-49 ||
And having presided over that form, Śambhu, Hara, whose sole vision is the welfare of others, [remained] for the sake of men. || 50 ||
Śambhu,
whose sole vision is the welfare of others, having taken recourse to a form that is the very nature of power (śakti) manifested in the image of the object of meditation,
brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation for those persons who— because their power is shrouded by impurity— are themselves incapable [of attaining them] due to their obstructed strength.

He brings about both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, he is called *Hara* because he removes the fetters (*pāśa*) from the bound souls (*paśu*), or because he removes them for the sake of their enjoyment.

As it is said—(this half-verse is seen cited in the *Netratantroddyota*, 1.3): "He removes the fetters from the bound souls and [leads] the person upward to the supreme state; therefore, he is *Hara*. And the application here is: *puruṣā*...

They are not capable of acting of their own accord for the sake of enjoyment or liberation, because, being bound, they lack independence—just like a sheep or other animals tied up. Furthermore, the fetters (pāśas) do not themselves act toward or away from the goal of the person (puruṣārtha), because they are insentient, like a rope or similar objects. Therefore, it is established that He who is the cause of their enjoyment and liberation is Śiva alone. || 50 ||
And in this regard:
"The state of being a Vidyā or a Vidyeśa is the lower liberation; here, in the higher [liberation], there is equality with Śiva. (51)

Although the states of the Vidyās and so forth are subject to impulsion with respect to supreme liberation, because they have transcended *māyā* and are stainless, there is no further connection to *saṃsāra*; thus, they constitute "inferior liberation. Equality with Śiva, however, is indeed supreme liberation alone. || 51 ||
And therefore:
Because they are worthy of universal pervasion, the mantras and other [powers] will indeed pervade.
Thus, the person whose power has been manifested by the Lord (pati) attains equality with that Lord.

The power of the atom, which was previously observed to conform to its manifestor, cannot be transferred because that power was already seen [to reside] there before; nor is it one and the same, like a universal (jāti).
The meaning is that the mantras and so forth are designated as "liberated" because they are worthy of supreme liberation. Now, one might object:

since the person is seen to possess only limited knowledge during the state of transmigratory existence, he must remain exactly like that even in liberation; to this, [the author] says: "manifested by the Lord. Because this person has had his power manifested by Śiva—who is omniscient and endowed with all powers—therefore, for him...

That equality indeed occurs. To explain: in the state of saṃsāra, according to the power of the manifesting conditions, the association with ignorance and so forth is seen in some, while the excellence of knowledge and so forth is seen in others. For this very reason, he states that even the doctrine of liberation through the transference of the qualities of Īśvara is untenable, saying "because it was previously observed" (*prāgdṛṣṭatvāt*). This refers to the case of the conscious person (*puruṣa-prājña*).

Because the power of knowledge and so forth is observed [to belong to the self], and because it is impossible for qualities to transfer into that which is formless, and because no such transfer is observed even when a transfer would otherwise be expected, the position of transference is untenable. Furthermore, this method of refuting liberation through transference and other such means was stated by the venerable Teacher: "There is no instance of an example to prove the transference of qualities; rather, from instruction, another consciousness of a similar kind is produced."

This has been established in detail in the *Śrīmadrauravavṛtti* by means of such verses as: "The arising [of a flame] in another fuel from a lamp occurs in another fuel; yet for that which is formless, there is neither a world nor an investigator regarding its transmigration" (*Pañcārthakārikā* 13–22).

Furthermore, that liberation, which consists in the state of equality with Śiva, is not a single entity like the universal *gotva* (cowness) and so forth; rather, it is distinct and resides in each individual person.

It has also been established in that very same place that a universal (jāti) is impossible apart from similarity; for, as stated, since persons are many, the liberation of one would entail the liberation of all. || 52-53 ||
He states that even liberation known as absorption into the Supreme Self (paramātma-laya) is not possible:
"Since persons have been perceived as distinct more than once, there can be no identity [of the individual with the Self] on that account either;
nor is there destruction of the person and the power [of consciousness] in liberation, because those two are beginningless. (54)

The connection is with what will be stated later, namely "in liberation" (*muktau*). He states—“And there is no destruction” (v. 54)—that even the absence of consciousness (*saṃvid*) as accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others in liberation is untenable, because both power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) are established as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and eternal.

For this very reason, because it is eternal due to being beginningless, the destruction of Śiva— who is the cause of liberation— and who exists as Śakti, or of His sovereignty, is impossible. Consequently, he states that the claim made by those who maintain the doctrine of a Successive Lord (pravāheśvara)— that through the destruction of that [bondage], His sovereignty arises in the liberated one— is untenable:
Nor is there an absence of Śiva, of His power, or of the efficient cause;
and because these are not separate from one another due to their nature as qualities, their perception is said to be indistinguishable, yet they possess specific distinctions.

Because Śiva and liberated souls possess identical qualities, their perception is described as being of one and the same nature and not distinct; that is, the manifestation of knowledge and so forth has all things as its object. To the question, "What then is the distinction of Śiva from these [liberated souls]? he says: "The distinction... (verse 55).

The majesty born of Śiva, which is without beginning, middle, or end, resides in those liberated souls; even though that majesty— consisting of omniscience and omnipotence— is itself without beginning, middle, or end, it becomes manifest through Śiva as its instrumental cause, since it was previously veiled by beginningless impurity.
Śiva, however, is endowed with beginningless omniscience and omnipotence; this is the distinction between him and these [others]. || 56 ||
Thus, Śambhu alone, the bestower of all boons, is to be propitiated by one who knows the truth.
When He is pleased, however, both supernatural power (*siddhi*) and supreme liberation (*mukti*) shall accrue to the person.

As it is stated in the *Atharvaśikhā*: "Śiva alone, the bringer of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon, having abandoned everything else" (1.2). Therefore, because He is the benefactor of all and the creator of all, the authority belongs solely to His scripture known as the Śaiva.
Because other scriptures, such as those of the Buddhists and others, were composed by non-omniscient beings and are therefore mutually contradictory. As they say—(see Mañjarī-pañjikā, p.
67, note 18, where this verse is cited as a statement of Bhaṭṭa Kumārila from the *Sarvajñasiddhi* in the *Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī*, p. 5): "If the Sugata is omniscient, why is Kapila not?"

[Objection: "If both [the Śaiva and the Buddhist] are omniscient, how can there be a difference of opinion between them? [Response: But surely, for the Śaiva as well, there is invalidity due to contradiction with other scriptures (*āgama*). That is not so, because there is no contradiction. For instance, this [Śaiva scripture] demonstrates the states attainable through all other scriptures and then reveals objects not previously understood by them.

Its authority is indeed incontestable. As they say: "A means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object not previously apprehended. Furthermore, [see the third footnote on page 129 of the previous section]. Because it does not contradict the Vedas—given such injunctions as "one should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought"—and because it is accepted by those who know the Vedas, its authority is established.

There is no state of being a heretic [in this practice], as there is not in other philosophical systems. Likewise, the performance of this rite by great sages such as Śveta and Upamanyu is heard of in the Purāṇas and Itihāsas; and in the Mahābhārata, it is recorded for Nara and Nārāyaṇa as well as for Aśvatthāman.

Furthermore, in the Suvarṇākṣa [Purāṇa], it is stated: "By you, O Deva, these two [Nara and Nārāyaṇa] have been worshipped in the form of Liṅgas, and Aśvatthāman in the form of an image (arcā), in age after age. This is because Viṣṇu was propitiated through that [Liṅga-worship].
And there is grace (*prasāda*). Furthermore, [it is said] in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "O Kṛṣṇa, nothing else in the world shall be dearer to me," and so forth.

In the *Smṛtis* concerning Kārtavīrya and others, there is Dharma preceded by the establishment [of shrines]: "He who properly constructs a temple of Śiva with baked bricks," and so forth. And in the Sūtra: "One should point out liberation (*mokṣa*)," and in the *Atharvaśiras*.

In the *Śvetāśvatara* and other Upaniṣads, the worship of the *liṅga* and other such practices are heard of. Consequently, there is no contradiction [with scripture] regarding this, nor is it devoid of a foundational source, nor is it accepted by only a few. Therefore, that statement must indeed be accepted, because it is uncontradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because it is the most excellent of all. And it has been said in the *Mokṣakārikā*: "Nor [is it contradicted] by any other means of valid cognition..."
"His range is restricted; therefore, even those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) should accept that which is a means for attaining a superior result. (Verse 146)
Now, he states by whom this treatise was composed:
"Thus spoke Sadyojyotis, the author of the excellent commentary (*suvṛtti*), regarding the principles (*tattvas*). (57)
Thus ends the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.
"Suvṛtti" and "Sadvṛtti" are names of the *Rauravavṛtti*; the meaning is that this was composed by its author. || 57 ||

By the venerable Śambhu, who is like the sun to the lotuses that are the illustrious Kheṭaka lineage, who has destroyed the mass of the darkness of ignorance with his words consisting of excellent conduct,
and who, being entreated with reverence by the best of wise men desiring to know the truth, [has composed this work].
A concise and clear commentary on the summary of the principles has been composed.
Thus ends the *Tattvasaṃgrahaṭīkā* composed by Aghoraśivācārya.
